type_specific.meeting_summary: The Arvada City Council held a budget workshop in which City Manager Don Wiek and Finance Director Brian Archer presented the proposed 2027–2028 two-year budget framework, covering the decision-making criteria used to prioritize spending, a conservative approach to new hires, and rising health care costs. Human Resources Director Gabriela Palmer detailed a recommended 3.86% overall compensation increase for 2027, while department directors from Community Development, Infrastructure, Organizational Services & Effectiveness, Police, and Vibrant Communities & Neighborhoods each outlined their priorities, funded requests, and emerging challenges. No formal votes were taken; the workshop was designed to inform future budget adoption at a regular business meeting.

workshop_topics.title: 2027–2028 Budget Framework & Decision Stack
workshop_topics.tagline: City manager lays out the philosophy behind this year's spending priorities
workshop_topics.lede: City Manager Don Wiek opened the workshop by describing two frameworks guiding the proposed budget: a 'decision stack' that ranks spending requests against mandatory costs, prior commitments, revenue trends, Council strategic alignment, and public value; and a set of staffing principles aimed at avoiding future layoffs. He noted that 106 positions had been added over the past six years and that staff reviewed every one of those roles before recommending only six new positions out of 32 requests.
workshop_topics.feeds_into: Future business meeting for formal budget adoption, expected late 2026

workshop_topics.title: Compensation & Health Care Costs
workshop_topics.tagline: Staff recommends 3.86% overall pay increase while health care costs surge nearly 16%
workshop_topics.lede: HR Director Gabriela Palmer and Finance Director Brian Archer presented the proposed 2027 compensation plan, which includes a 2% market-range adjustment for all employees in January, step increases for eligible staff (roughly 70% of the workforce), and larger step increases for police officers (7.25%). Health care costs originally projected to rise 22% were reduced to 15.9% through plan design changes negotiated with the benefits consultant; a portion of the health care fund reserve will be used to offset the remaining increase without eliminating any covered services.

options.label: Recommended compensation plan (3.86% overall increase)
options.summary: All employees receive a 2% market range adjustment; roughly 70% also receive step increases of 2%–3.75% (police steps up to 7.25%); 32 employees receive reclassification adjustments. Health care premium increase held to 15.9% via plan redesign and partial draw on the health care fund reserve.
options.endorsement: Staff recommendation; no council member opposed

workshop_topics.feeds_into: Future business meeting for formal budget and salary plan adoption, expected late 2026

workshop_topics.title: New Position Requests (Six Funded Roles)
workshop_topics.tagline: Staff recommends six new positions out of 32 requests, plus three COPS-grant officers
workshop_topics.lede: Finance Director Brian Archer reviewed the six positions recommended for funding in the 2027–2028 budget: a Homelessness Resolution Case Manager (moved from HODAG fund to General Fund for permanent funding), a Records Management System Consortium coordinator (shared with Lakewood, also supports body camera program), an Emergency Management Specialist (grant-funded for up to three years), a Parks Maintenance Worker for graffiti abatement, three police officers funded via a federal COPS grant (covering 75% of salary for three years up to $125,000 each), and a Stormwater Inspector Supervisor. City Manager Wiek noted that all 106 positions added over the past six years are being reviewed before any additional hires are approved.

options.label: Six recommended new positions (plus 3 COPS-grant officers)
options.cost: Cost TBD (embedded in departmental budget lines)
options.summary: Adds a permanent Homelessness Case Manager to the General Fund, a Records Management System coordinator, a grant-funded Emergency Management Specialist, a Parks graffiti worker, three COPS-grant police officers, and a Stormwater Inspector Supervisor.
options.endorsement: Staff recommendation; council members did not object

workshop_topics.feeds_into: Future business meeting for formal budget adoption, expected late 2026

workshop_topics.title: Community Development Department Budget
workshop_topics.tagline: Focus on permitting software upgrade, housing services funding shift, and development coordination
workshop_topics.lede: Community Development Director Jessica Garner outlined the department's priorities, including implementation of the new SPARK permitting software (launching June or July 2027 with Nebulogic), a new Development Liaison Coordinator position (created through reclassification) to guide applicants through the permitting process, and a shift of a portion of CDBG grant funding to the General Fund to better support Human Services grants. Staff also flagged that the HODAG fund is nearly depleted and will need ongoing council attention.

options.label: Funded requests as proposed
options.cost: Includes $25,000/yr for part-time permits tech, SPARK annual maintenance, and Human Services grant funding shift
options.summary: Approves annual SPARK software maintenance fees, continues a 30-hr/week temporary permits technician, shifts Human Services grants from CDBG to the General Fund, and permanently funds the Homelessness Case Manager from the General Fund instead of HODAG.

workshop_topics.feeds_into: Future business meeting for formal budget adoption, expected late 2026

workshop_topics.title: Infrastructure Department Budget
workshop_topics.tagline: Street repaving milestone near, street light acquisition studied, utility costs rising
workshop_topics.lede: Infrastructure Director Jaclyn Rhodes reported that the city has repaved 73 of 75 targeted trail miles and is close to completing that strategic goal. She described ongoing work on traffic signal timing improvements, a multi-disciplinary team studying the potential purchase of Xcel Energy street lights (a decision expected within the coming year), rising utility and parking enforcement costs, and a proposed new Stormwater Inspector Supervisor position to improve inspection speed and accuracy. Staff also noted that capital funds from the 98-101 program are being used for the first time to supplement street maintenance funding, growing from $500,000 to $1 million.
workshop_topics.feeds_into: Future business meeting for formal budget adoption and potential street light acquisition presentation, expected 2027

workshop_topics.title: Organizational Services & Effectiveness (OSE) Budget
workshop_topics.tagline: AI threats, workforce succession, federal funding uncertainty, and $1.85M in new requests
workshop_topics.lede: OSE Director (name not stated in transcript, identified as 'Miss Cheek' by Mayor Simpson) presented $1.85 million in new General Fund expenditures covering continuation of the 40X strategic plan, a future ballot-measure engagement process, lobbying contract renewals, an Emergency Management Specialist (funded from General Fund in 2028), homelessness case management software, the Block-by-Block Olde Town ambassador program (launching October 1), a new City Attorney case management system (2028), and IT investments including a temporary applications systems officer to cover work during SPARK implementation and a new computer deployment tool replacing a Microsoft product going end-of-life.

options.label: Funded OSE requests as proposed
options.cost: $1.85 million total new expenditures (General Fund and IT Fund combined)
options.summary: Funds strategic plan continuation, ballot engagement preparation, lobbying, Olde Town ambassadors, homelessness data system, prosecutorial case management (2028), temporary IT staffing during SPARK rollout, and a new endpoint deployment tool.

workshop_topics.feeds_into: IGA for Lakewood Navigation Center expected to come before council as a formal action item; ballot measure engagement timeline subject to council direction

workshop_topics.title: Police & Municipal Court Budget
workshop_topics.tagline: Court caseload doubled; police flag training space, tech evaluation, and state mandate costs
workshop_topics.lede: Police Deputy Chief Todd Reeves and Municipal Court Judge Kurtz presented funding needs driven by mandatory cost increases: court-appointed attorney fees rose $10/hour under a legislative mandate, annual case volume roughly doubled from about 5,000 to 10,000 cases requiring more attorney and interpreter hours and additional case-management software subscriptions, and the Jeffco Crime Lab and Victim Outreach Incorporated contracts increased. Reeves also highlighted a shortage of training space at the Bickford Center, challenges obtaining federal grants due to conflicts between Colorado state law and federal requirements, and the department's ongoing work to evaluate community sentiment before deploying new technology.

options.label: Funded mandatory and contractual increases
options.cost: $40,000 additional for court subscriptions and attorney/interpreter contracts; additional amounts for VOI and Jeffco Crime Lab (amounts stated as mandatory increases)
options.summary: Covers required increases in court-appointed attorney rates, interpreter fees, case management software subscriptions for two courtrooms, and contractual increases for Victim Outreach Inc. and the Jeffco Crime Lab.
options.endorsement: Staff recommendation; council expressed no opposition

workshop_topics.feeds_into: Bailiff/court security officer solution expected to return as a staffing recommendation; formal budget adoption at a future business meeting

workshop_topics.title: Vibrant Communities & Neighborhoods (VCN) Budget
workshop_topics.tagline: Graffiti crew, drone fireworks, goats for vegetation management, and Kendall Whittenberg transition planning
workshop_topics.lede: VCN Director Greg Stevenson presented approximately $1 million in funded requests covering parks operations ($475,000), golf operations ($590,000), and several new initiatives: a graffiti abatement team modeled on the Adams County IGA program, a drone light-show pilot for the Fourth of July in place of traditional fireworks, a small goat herd for eco-friendly vegetation management, and long-range planning for the 2035 Kendall Whittenberg open-space transfer. Staff also flagged the near-depletion of the HODAG housing fund and the ongoing Apex parks services integration.

options.label: Funded VCN requests as proposed (~$1M)
options.summary: Funds graffiti abatement workers, a drone fireworks program, goat vegetation management pilot, golf operations costs (insurance, software, seasonal wages, credit card fees), and ongoing parks maintenance expenses.

workshop_topics.feeds_into: Median/Wadsworth corridor improvement funding expected to be addressed through capital and 98-101 programs; formal budget adoption at a future business meeting

workshop_topics.title: Ten-Year Financial Model Outlook
workshop_topics.tagline: General Fund deficit projected by 2034–2036, but seven years of runway remain
workshop_topics.lede: Finance Director Brian Archer closed the budget presentation with the updated ten-year financial models for all eleven city funds. For the General Fund, the prior model showed a roughly $21 million deficit by 2034; the proposed 2027–2028 budget reduces that projected deficit to approximately $9 million, though adding two more model years (2035–2036) shows a return to negative territory in the final year. Archer noted the city is not currently in a negative fund-balance position and has until approximately 2033 before it would exceed its reserve target, providing seven years to make adjustments.
workshop_topics.feeds_into: Future business meeting for formal budget adoption, expected late 2026

workshop_topics.title: Drought Update & Water Restrictions
workshop_topics.tagline: Lawn watering ends October 1; city has achieved 18% reduction over recent months
workshop_topics.lede: Infrastructure Director Jaclyn Rhodes provided a brief drought update at the close of the meeting: under the city's raw water contract with Denver Water, all lawn irrigation must cease by October 1, 2026. Staff is coordinating with schools and internal VCN teams to monitor high-use areas during the transition. Rhodes reported the city has achieved an 18% water use reduction over the most recent two months (and 14% averaged over the full season since April 15). Denver Water is also considering a drought emergency raw water rate, which its board will consider in October; staff will report to council on the pricing implications for 2027.
workshop_topics.feeds_into: Denver Water drought pricing decision expected October 2026; council briefing on 2027 rate impact to follow
